workflows.workflow_name: Slow System Performance & High Resource Usage (Cross-OS)
workflows.description: Cross-OS diagnostic workflow for identifying CPU, RAM, Disk I/O, storage capacity, or OS-level log bottlenecks on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

safety_red_flags.label: Extreme overheating (burning hot chassis), grinding/clicking hard drive sounds, or burning smell
safety_red_flags.warning_message: SAFETY STOP: Severe thermal or mechanical storage failure suspected. Continuing heavy workloads may cause permanent hardware damage or data loss.
safety_red_flags.escalation_instruction: Back up critical open files if safe, shut down the system immediately, and escalate to hardware support.

steps.title: Measure Overall CPU, Memory, and Disk Utilization
steps.objective: Identify which primary system resource (CPU, RAM, or Disk) is saturated so troubleshooting targets the actual bottleneck.
instructions: Open the system resource monitor for your operating system.
Observe overall CPU %, Memory usage / pressure, and Disk activity % for 15-30 seconds.
Record which resource is consistently pegged high (e.g., > 85-90%).
Press `Ctrl + Shift + Esc` to open Task Manager.
Click the 'Performance' tab (or run `perfmon /res` for Resource Monitor).
Check sustained CPU %, Memory %, and Disk Active Time %.
windows.expected_output_hint: Normal idle/light use: CPU < 30%, Memory < 75%, Disk < 20%

instructions: Open Terminal and run `top` (press `q` to quit) or `htop` if installed.
Check `%Cpu(s)` (specifically `us`, `sy`, and `wa` for I/O wait), `MiB Mem`, and `load average`.
linux.expected_output_hint: Low CPU idle (`id` < 15%) = CPU bottleneck; high `wa` = Disk I/O bottleneck

instructions: Open Spotlight (`Cmd + Space`) and launch 'Activity Monitor'.
Check the CPU tab (% Idle), Memory tab (Memory Pressure graph: Green/Yellow/Red), and Disk tab.
Or run the read-only terminal snapshot below.
macos.expected_output_hint: Memory Pressure should be Green; CPU Idle > 50% at light load

steps.expected_results: CPU, Memory, and Disk utilization remain within normal operating thresholds without sustained saturation.
safety_requirements: Read-only monitoring step. Do not force-terminate unfamiliar system processes yet.

learning_content.why_this_step: Slowness is a symptom, not a root cause. Measuring CPU, RAM, and Disk first prevents blind fixes like rebooting or reinstalling software without knowing what is actually bottlenecked.
learning_content.technical_principle: Operating systems schedule CPU time, physical RAM (plus pagefile/swap), and storage I/O queues. Saturation in any one subsystem creates lag across all applications, including mouse/UI responsiveness.
learning_content.limitations: A single instant snapshot can miss intermittent spikes; observe for at least 15-30 seconds while the slowness occurs.

outcomes.label: CPU usage is consistently very high (> 85%) or Linux load average is well above core count

transition.summary: CPU saturation detected. Proceed to identify the top CPU-consuming process.

outcomes.label: Memory usage is > 90%, heavy swap/paging occurs, or macOS Memory Pressure is Yellow/Red
outcomes.finding_hint: High memory pressure / RAM exhaustion observed.

transition.summary: Memory bottleneck detected. Proceed to inspect RAM and swap consumers.

outcomes.label: Disk active time is stuck near 100%, Linux I/O wait (`wa`) is high, or system warns of low disk space
outcomes.finding_hint: Storage I/O saturation or capacity bottleneck observed.

transition.summary: Storage bottleneck detected. Proceed to inspect free disk space and I/O.

outcomes.label: CPU, Memory, and Disk utilization all look normal, yet the system still feels sluggish or freezes
outcomes.finding_hint: System feels slow despite normal resource gauges; suspect thermal throttling, driver stalls, or OS errors.

transition.summary: Proceed to inspect OS system logs for hardware, thermal, or driver errors.

inconclusive.summary: Record approximate CPU %, Memory %, and Disk % while the slowdown is happening.

not_performed.summary: Workflow paused pending resource utilization check.

unable_to_perform.summary: System is too unresponsive to open monitoring tools; escalate to L2 Support.

steps.title: Identify Top CPU-Consuming Processes
steps.objective: Determine whether high CPU usage is caused by a user application (e.g., browser tab, video call) or an OS/background system process.
instructions: Sort running processes by CPU usage descending.
Record the top 1-3 process names and their CPU percentages.
Determine if the top consumer is a normal user application or a core OS/background service.
In Task Manager > Processes tab, click the 'CPU' column header to sort highest first.
Or run the PowerShell read-only command below to list the top 10 processes by CPU time.
windows.expected_output_hint: Identifies the exact process name (e.g., chrome, Teams, TiWorker, Antimalware Service)

instructions: Open Terminal and run `ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -n 11`.
Note the USER, PID, %CPU, and COMMAND columns of the top entries.
linux.expected_output_hint: Top process and PID consuming CPU are clearly listed

instructions: In Activity Monitor > CPU tab, click '% CPU' to sort descending.
Or run `ps aux -r | head -n 11` in Terminal.
macos.gui_path: Activity Monitor > CPU tab (sort by % CPU)
macos.expected_output_hint: Identifies whether a user app or system daemon (e.g., kernel_task, mds_stores) is spiking

steps.expected_results: The specific process or service responsible for high CPU utilization is clearly identified.
safety_requirements: Read-only inspection. Never kill core OS processes (e.g., `System`, `csrss.exe`, `systemd`, `kernel_task`) as doing so can crash the OS.

learning_content.why_this_step: Distinguishing a runaway user app from a system daemon changes the fix completely: a hung browser tab can be safely closed, whereas high `kernel_task` (macOS) or `System Interrupts` (Windows) often indicates thermal throttling or faulty hardware/drivers.
learning_content.technical_principle: User-space processes run in unprivileged rings and can be restarted safely; kernel/system services manage hardware interrupts, indexing, updates, and thermal protection.
learning_content.limitations: High CPU from background updates (Windows Update `TiWorker`, Linux `apt`/`unattended-upgrades`, macOS Spotlight `mds_stores`) may be normal temporary maintenance rather than a fault.

outcomes.label: A specific user application (e.g., browser, IDE, meeting app) is consuming most CPU
outcomes.finding_hint: Evidence-supported high CPU caused by a user-space application. Advise saving work, restarting or updating the application, and checking browser extensions.

transition.summary: CPU bottleneck isolated to a specific user application.

outcomes.label: An OS/system process (e.g., System Interrupts, kernel_task, kworker, Antimalware) is dominating CPU
outcomes.finding_hint: High CPU is driven by an OS kernel/system process; inspect system logs for driver, thermal, or update faults.

transition.summary: Proceed to inspect system logs for driver, thermal, or OS service errors.

inconclusive.summary: Record the exact top 3 process names and their CPU %.

unable_to_perform.summary: Unable to inspect running processes; escalate to L2 Support.

steps.title: Inspect Memory Pressure, Swap Usage, and Top RAM Consumers
steps.objective: Determine whether RAM exhaustion is caused by normal heavy multi-tasking or an abnormal memory leak.
instructions: Check total physical RAM, available RAM, and swap/pagefile usage.
Sort processes by Memory usage descending and record the top 3 consumers.
Open Task Manager > Processes tab and sort by 'Memory'.
Check Performance > Memory for 'In use', 'Available', and 'Committed' values.
windows.gui_path: Task Manager > Processes (sort by Memory) & Performance > Memory
windows.expected_output_hint: Lists top RAM-consuming processes in MB

instructions: Run `free -h` to inspect `available` RAM and `Swap` usage (note: `buff/cache` is normal reclaimable cache, not wasted RAM).
Run `ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 11` to list top memory consumers.
linux.expected_output_hint: Look at 'available' column in `free -h`, not 'free', and check if Swap used is high

instructions: Open Activity Monitor > Memory tab, sort by 'Memory', and check 'Memory Pressure' and 'Swap Used' at the bottom.
Or run `memory_pressure` in Terminal.
macos.expected_output_hint: Shows system-wide free memory percentage and pressure level

steps.expected_results: Identifies whether heavy user applications or an abnormal OS/kernel memory leak is causing swap thrashing.
safety_requirements: Read-only inspection. Remind users to save unsaved documents before closing memory-heavy applications.

learning_content.why_this_step: When physical RAM fills up, the OS moves memory pages to slower disk swap/pagefile ('thrashing'), making the entire computer feel frozen even when CPU usage is low.
learning_content.technical_principle: Modern OSes intentionally use free RAM for disk caching (Linux `buff/cache`, macOS Cached Files, Windows Standby). True memory exhaustion is indicated by low *Available* RAM, high *Swap/Pagefile* activity, or Yellow/Red Memory Pressure.
learning_content.limitations: Closing apps relieves immediate pressure, but if the user's daily workload consistently exceeds installed RAM (e.g., 8 GB RAM running VMs + 50 browser tabs), a hardware RAM upgrade may be needed.

outcomes.label: Multiple heavy user apps (e.g., browsers, Docker, VMs, creative tools) account for almost all RAM usage
outcomes.finding_hint: Evidence-supported RAM exhaustion and swap thrashing due to active user workload exceeding available physical memory.

transition.summary: Advise closing unused heavy applications/tabs, disabling unnecessary startup apps, or evaluating a RAM upgrade.

outcomes.label: High RAM/swap usage with no obvious user app responsible (possible driver/kernel memory leak)
outcomes.finding_hint: Suspected OS, service, or driver memory leak; inspect system logs next.

transition.summary: Proceed to inspect system logs for OOM killer events, driver errors, or memory warnings.

inconclusive.summary: Record total RAM, available RAM/memory pressure, swap usage, and top 3 memory processes.

unable_to_perform.summary: Unable to inspect memory statistics; escalate to L2 Support.

steps.title: Check Free Disk Space and Storage I/O Activity
steps.objective: Verify whether the system drive is critically full (< 10% free) or experiencing abnormal disk I/O saturation.
instructions: Check available free space on the primary OS drive/partition.
Check whether disk read/write activity is pegged at 100%.
Check free space on `C:` in File Explorer or Settings > System > Storage.
Or run the PowerShell command below to check drive capacity and free space.
windows.gui_path: Settings > System > Storage (and Task Manager > Performance > Disk)
windows.expected_output_hint: System drive (C:) should have at least 10-15% free space

instructions: Run `df -h` in Terminal and inspect the `Use%` column for `/` and `/home`.
Optionally check `df -i` if inode exhaustion is suspected.
Open System Settings > General > Storage to view available space.
Or run `df -h /` in Terminal.
macos.expected_output_hint: Primary volume should have at least 15-20 GB (or > 10%) free

steps.expected_results: Primary OS drive has > 10-15% free space and normal disk I/O latency.
safety_requirements: Read-only check. Always recommend backing up important user data before deleting files or running disk repair tools.

learning_content.why_this_step: Nearly full SSDs and OS partitions severely degrade write performance, prevent swap/pagefile expansion, and can stop OS updates or login sessions from functioning.
learning_content.technical_principle: SSDs require free blocks for wear-leveling and garbage collection; operating systems also need free space for virtual memory swap files, logs, and temporary caches.
learning_content.limitations: Adequate free space does not rule out a failing HDD/SSD with bad sectors or a buggy storage driver; check system logs if disk I/O remains stuck at 100%.

outcomes.label: System drive is critically full (< 10% free or < 5 GB remaining)
outcomes.finding_hint: Evidence-supported critical low disk space on the OS volume causing severe performance degradation.

transition.summary: Back up critical files first, then safely free disk space (clear trash/temp files, uninstall unused apps, or archive large media) to restore > 15% free capacity.

outcomes.label: Plenty of free disk space (> 15% free), but disk I/O remains stuck very high
outcomes.finding_hint: High storage I/O despite adequate free space; suspect failing drive, background indexing/scan, or storage driver issue.

transition.summary: Proceed to inspect OS system logs for disk/I/O errors or SMART warnings.

inconclusive.summary: Record the exact total size and free space percentage of the primary OS drive.

not_performed.summary: Workflow paused pending disk space and I/O check.

unable_to_perform.summary: Unable to inspect storage metrics; escalate to L2 Support.

steps.title: Inspect OS System Logs for Hardware, Storage, Thermal, or Driver Errors
steps.objective: Collect concrete OS log evidence of recurring errors (e.g., disk bad blocks, OOM killer, thermal throttling, or crashing services).
instructions: Open the OS system log viewer or run the read-only log query command.
Look for repeated Error or Critical entries within the last 30 minutes to 24 hours (especially disk, kernel, thermal, or driver faults).
Open Event Viewer (`eventvwr.msc`) > Windows Logs > System and filter for Critical and Error events.
Or run the PowerShell read-only command below to inspect the latest 20 System errors.
windows.expected_output_hint: Look for recurring Disk (Event ID 7/51/129), Kernel-Power, or Driver errors

instructions: Open Terminal and run `journalctl -p err -n 30 --no-pager` to review recent system error logs.
Optionally run `dmesg -T --level=err,warn | tail -n 20` for kernel/hardware messages.
linux.expected_output_hint: Look for I/O errors (`blk_update_request`), `Out of memory` (OOM), or thermal throttle messages

instructions: Open Applications > Utilities > Console to inspect crash reports and system errors.
Or run the read-only `log show` command below to list recent error-level log entries.
macos.gui_path: Applications > Utilities > Console > Crash Reports / system.log
macos.expected_output_hint: Look for recurring disk I/O errors, kernel extensions, or thermal/watchdog warnings

steps.expected_results: No recurring critical hardware, disk, kernel, or driver errors appear in recent system logs.
safety_requirements: Read-only log inspection. Do not run destructive OS reset or disk repair commands before backing up user data.

learning_content.why_this_step: System logs provide timestamped, authoritative evidence that visual observation cannot reveal—such as silent disk read retries, Linux OOM kills, or Windows driver resets—making L1-to-L2 escalation dramatically faster.
learning_content.technical_principle: All major operating systems maintain centralized event logging daemons (Windows Event Log, Linux systemd-journald, macOS Unified Logging) that capture kernel, driver, and service faults.
learning_content.limitations: Logs can contain benign background warnings; correlate error timestamps directly with when the user experienced slowness.

outcomes.label: Recurring Critical/Error entries found (e.g., Disk I/O error, OOM kill, Thermal throttle, or Driver crash)
outcomes.finding_hint: Evidence-supported OS/hardware fault recorded in system logs. Attach exact log excerpts/Event IDs to the escalation report.

transition.summary: Escalate to L2 Support with captured system log excerpts (and recommend immediate data backup if disk errors are present).

outcomes.label: No recurring critical errors in system logs despite persistent slowness
outcomes.finding_hint: No critical OS log faults detected; deeper L2 diagnostics needed (e.g., malware scan, SMART drive health, BIOS/thermal check, or profile corruption).

transition.summary: Escalate to L2 Support with resource metrics and clean log verification for deeper profiling.

inconclusive.summary: Copy the most recent 5-10 error lines or Event IDs from the log viewer.

not_performed.summary: Workflow paused pending system log inspection.

unable_to_perform.summary: Insufficient privileges or unable to read system logs; escalate to L2 Support.
